title: A Verdict for the Autopsy
premise: Rosalind Montrose, the reclusive coroner of Hollow Creek, has spent years quietly correcting the record on deaths the town preferred to forget. When a confession letter arrives for a man already buried—postmarked the day after his funeral—she realizes someone is using her own methods against her, threading her three 'solved' accidents into a pattern that points back to a fire thirty years ago. As she digs into alibis woven by the town's founding families, Rosalind discovers the letter's author is dying and racing her to expose the truth before the last witness, or the last suspect, is silenced. In the end, Rosalind must choose between protecting her anonymity and testifying openly, and in doing so finds the found family she never believed she deserved.
about_author: Kestrel Sandoval spent a decade as a rural paramedic in the Appalachian foothills, where small-town secrets were as common as kudzu. A Verdict for the Autopsy is their first novel, drawn from a career of listening to what the dead could no longer say.

chapters.title: The Letter That Outlived Him
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Days after burying Edwin Voss, Rosalind receives a confession letter postmarked after his death, confessing to a drowning she'd quietly ruled accidental years ago. The letter references all three of her secret corrections. Emotional beat: unease—the invisible life she built is being read like an open book.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Signature
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She rereads her old case files and finds each of the three deaths connects to the 1994 Harrow House fire, which killed one girl and was ruled electrical. The letter writer knew details never made public. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose; her quiet vigilante work has summoned something older and larger.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with a flashback to young Deputy Amara Cole (now sheriff) at the fire scene. Rosalind reluctantly brings Amara in; they map the five surviving members of the families who owned Harrow House. Each has an alibi thirty years old—and each alibi depends on another family member lying. Emotional beat: wary alliance, two women who've guarded the same secrets from opposite sides.

chapters.title: What the Grave Keeps
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Exhumation of the fire victim, Tessa Harrow, reveals smoke inhalation inconsistent with the official story—she was dead before the flames. Someone in town helped falsify the original autopsy. Emotional beat: violation and resolve; the corruption reaches into her own profession's history.

chapters.title: Alibi in Amber
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Rosalind interviewing suspects, intercut with 1994 flashbacks from teenage Tessa. We learn Tessa planned to run away with a boy from outside the family circle, carrying evidence of the families' fraud. Emotional beat: sympathy deepening into grief—Tessa becomes a person, not a case number.

chapters.title: The Dying Hand
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Tracing the letter's paper and typewriter ribbon, she narrows the author to Mortimer Hale, a retired judge now in hospice—who admits he wrote it but refuses to name who killed Tessa, insisting Rosalind must earn the truth herself. He gives her a key to a bank box. Emotional beat: frustration curdling into urgency as Hale's health fails.

chapters.title: A Threat With Good Manners
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Anonymous warnings escalate: her office is searched, her cat disappears and returns unharmed—a message, not an accident. Amara reveals she was pressured to close the fire case in '94 and has carried the shame since. Emotional beat: fear, but also the first crack of genuine trust between Rosalind and Amara.

chapters.title: The Bank Box
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The box holds Tessa's evidence of the families' land-fraud scheme and a photograph proving her death was staged to look like the fire claimed her—but the body in the grave isn't Tessa's. The real Tessa may have lived. Emotional beat: vertigo; every certainty about the case collapses, and hope arrives in the most unsettling form.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Climax. Rosalind's POV. At the Harrow estate, she confronts the surviving matriarch, Vivian Ashcombe, who confesses: her son killed the boy Tessa loved, and Tessa fled with the family's complicity—while an unidentified runaway died in her place. Vivian's hired hand tries to silence Rosalind; Amara arrives, having followed her. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into courage as Rosalind chooses to be seen.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, epilogue weeks later. Testimony given, arrests made, Tessa located alive under a new name and reunited with the truth. The town knows Rosalind now—not as the invisible coroner but as their own. Amara stays for Sunday dinner. Emotional beat: belonging; the woman who knew every grave finally learns what it is to be known.
